results.title: Forecasting Major Risks from AI
results.content:
This post covers key highlights from the Wave 9 LEAP survey that we conducted between May 19 and June 10, 2026. Recent waves covered robotics, the economic effects of AI, security and geopolitics, AI R&D, and AI timelines. More information about Wave 9, including question details and analysis of rationales, is available here.

### Insight 1: Experts and superforecasters think a major AI-driven harm event is more likely than not by 2050 [...] In 2025, the FBI reported nearly $21 billion in financial losses from cyber-enabled crime—more than double the figure in 2022 ($10.3 billion). If AI capabilities progress slowly through 2030, the median expert predicts that losses reported to the FBI will increase to $25 billion in 2026, $35 billion in 2028, and $46 billion in 2031. If AI progress is rapid by 2030, they predict reported losses of $31 billion, $50 billion, and $70 billion, respectively. In a rapid-progress world, experts give a [...] We also asked forecasters to predict the likelihood of a global AI-related catastrophe in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period. If AI capabilities progress slowly, the median expert assigns this a 0.08% probability by 2030, 1% by 2050, and 2% by 2100. In a scenario where AI progress by 2030 is rapid, those forecasts rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%.1

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I start from base rates: already-observed cyber losses are large enough that AI-enabled cyber dominates the low-severity, near-term AI incident ladders, while engineered-bio and loss-of-control AI drive most of the far-tail mortality risk. Expert and superforecaster evidence remains widely dispersed; I anchor between XPT-style superforecaster and domain-expert estimates, with near-term probabilities kept low because no current systems appear capable of autonomously causing mass casualties, but rising sharply as frontier systems become more agentic and embedded in cyber, science, and infrastructure. Policies that slow capability development or add binding pre-release authorization reduce risk most before 2050; unilateral US action helps but less than US-China/international measures, and federal preemption modestly increases risk by removing state-level safety experimentation. For 2100, I reduce the effect of policies that expire in 2050 but allow persistence through slower diffusion, better institutions, and safer development paths. General catastrophe includes non-AI nuclear, pandemic, climate/ecological and other causes, so AI-specific policies move it less than they move AI catastrophe and disempowerment.

results.title: Assessing Near-Term Accuracy in the Existential Risk ...
results.content: The median expert in the XPT forecast a 20% probability of global catastrophe—defined as a loss of at least 10% of the global population—and a 6% probability of human extinction by 2100. Superforecasters viewed the world as less risky, forecasting a 9% and 1% probability of global catastrophe and human extinction by 2100, respectively. This held across domains, though not uniformly: superforecasters and experts were much further apart on risk related to AI than on the risk of nuclear war. [...] Overall, our findings challenge the hope that near-term accuracy can reliably identify forecasters with more credible long-term risk predictions. These results are consistent with the analysis from the original XPT report. The original XPT report found that, for “AI-concerned” (the third of participants with the highest forecast of AI extinction risk by 2100) and “AI-skeptic” (the third of participants with the lowest forecast of AI extinction risk by 2100) groups, their near-term forecasts [...] Respondents underestimated AI progress, especially superforecasters. XPT participants significantly underestimated the pace of AI advancement across multiple benchmarks. For three standard AI benchmarks—MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY—domain experts assigned probabilities of 21.4%, 25.0%, and 43.5% respectively to the outcomes achieved by the end of 2024. Superforecasters were even more pessimistic, assigning only 9.3%, 7.2%, and 20.1% respectively. The International Mathematical Olympiad results

results.title: Forecasting Major Risks from AI
results.content: We also asked respondents for the probability of a global catastrophe from any cause—again defining catastrophe as the death of more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period. Conditional on AI capabilities progressing rapidly by 2030, the median expert forecasts the probability of an AI-related catastrophe by 2100 at 10% compared with 15% for a catastrophe from any cause. [...] We also asked forecasters to predict the likelihood of a global AI-related catastrophe in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period. If AI capabilities progress slowly, the median expert assigns this a 0.08% probability by 2030, 1% by 2050, and 2% by 2100. In a scenario where AI progress by 2030 is rapid, those forecasts rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%.1 [...] We computed each respondent’s ratio of AI catastrophic risk to total catastrophic risk. The median expert attributes about two-thirds (67%) of total global catastrophic risk to AI in a world where AI capabilities progress rapidly, but roughly 30% in a slow progress world.

rationale: I start from base rates: already-observed cyber losses are large enough that AI-enabled cyber dominates the low-severity, near-term AI incident ladders, while engineered-bio and loss-of-control AI drive most of the far-tail mortality risk. Expert and superforecaster evidence remains widely dispersed; I anchor between XPT-style superforecaster and domain-expert estimates, with near-term probabilities kept low because no current systems appear capable of autonomously causing mass casualties, but rising sharply as frontier systems become more agentic and embedded in cyber, science, and infrastructure. Policies that slow capability development or add binding pre-release authorization reduce risk most before 2050; unilateral US action helps but less than US-China/international measures, and federal preemption modestly increases risk by removing state-level safety experimentation. For 2100, I reduce the effect of policies that expire in 2050 but allow persistence through slower diffusion, better institutions, and safer development paths. General catastrophe includes non-AI nuclear, pandemic, climate/ecological and other causes, so AI-specific policies move it less than they move AI catastrophe and disempowerment.

rationale: I start from base rates: already-observed cyber losses are large enough that AI-enabled cyber dominates the low-severity, near-term AI incident ladders, while engineered-bio and loss-of-control AI drive most of the far-tail mortality risk. Expert and superforecaster evidence remains widely dispersed; I anchor between XPT-style superforecaster and domain-expert estimates, with near-term probabilities kept low because no current systems appear capable of autonomously causing mass casualties, but rising sharply as frontier systems become more agentic and embedded in cyber, science, and infrastructure. Policies that slow capability development or add binding pre-release authorization reduce risk most before 2050; unilateral US action helps but less than US-China/international measures, and federal preemption modestly increases risk by removing state-level safety experimentation. For 2100, I reduce the effect of policies that expire in 2050 but allow persistence through slower diffusion, better institutions, and safer development paths. General catastrophe includes non-AI nuclear, pandemic, climate/ecological and other causes, so AI-specific policies move it less than they move AI catastrophe and disempowerment.

rationale: I start from base rates: already-observed cyber losses are large enough that AI-enabled cyber dominates the low-severity, near-term AI incident ladders, while engineered-bio and loss-of-control AI drive most of the far-tail mortality risk. Expert and superforecaster evidence remains widely dispersed; I anchor between XPT-style superforecaster and domain-expert estimates, with near-term probabilities kept low because no current systems appear capable of autonomously causing mass casualties, but rising sharply as frontier systems become more agentic and embedded in cyber, science, and infrastructure. Policies that slow capability development or add binding pre-release authorization reduce risk most before 2050; unilateral US action helps but less than US-China/international measures, and federal preemption modestly increases risk by removing state-level safety experimentation. For 2100, I reduce the effect of policies that expire in 2050 but allow persistence through slower diffusion, better institutions, and safer development paths. General catastrophe includes non-AI nuclear, pandemic, climate/ecological and other causes, so AI-specific policies move it less than they move AI catastrophe and disempowerment.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I base my forecasts on current trends in AI capabilities, cyber vulnerabilities, and historical base rates for catastrophes. AI-related cyber incidents are the most likely near-term risk, given the rapid integration of AI into coding and hacking tools, leading to high probabilities for the $1B threshold by 2030. Bio and misalignment risks have lower base rates but scale significantly over longer horizons (2050, 2100) as capabilities approach AGI. The policy conditions (p1-p5) have varying effects: p1 (preemption) slightly increases risk by removing state regulations, while p2b (US+China compute cap) and p5 (bundle) significantly reduce risk by slowing frontier development and imposing strict liability. The effects of these policies compound over time, showing the largest risk reductions in the 2030-2050 window.

results.title: What could small scale disasters from AI look like? — LessWrong
results.content:
I'm asking because I'm curious about potential fire-alarm scenarios (including things which just help to make AI risks salient to the wider public), and also looking to operationalise a forecasting question which is currently drafted as

By 2032, will we see an event precipitated by AI that causes at least 100 deaths and/or at least $1B 2021 USD in economic damage?

to allow a clear and sensible resolution.

# 3 Answers sorted by top scoring

Anon User

### Aug 31, 2021 [...] # 14

Some high-profile failures I think we won't get are related to convergent goals, such as acquiring computing power, deceiving humans into not editing you, etc. We'll probably get examples of this sort of thing in small scale experiments, that specialists might hear about, but if an AI that's deceptive for instrumental reasons causes $1bn in damages I think it will be rather too late to learn our lesson. Boeing MCAS () is blaimed by more than 100 deaths. How much "AI" would a similar system need to include for a similar tragedy to count as "an event precipitated by AI"?

rationale: Base rates first: AI-enabled fraud/cyber losses are already ~$1-2B+/yr reported (FBI IC3 ~$0.9B AI-assisted in 2025, deepfake fraud $1.65B in 2025, Deloitte projects $40B GenAI fraud by 2027), so cumulative low-dollar thresholds ($1B, then $10B) for AI-related and AI-cyber incidents are near-locked-in over short horizons, while death-based and $100B+ thresholds require qualitatively larger events (grid/worm-scale attacks, engineered pandemics, autonomous-agent failures) that have never occurred; the first AI-orchestrated espionage campaign (Anthropic, Nov 2025) shows capability trending up but realized damage remains modest. Bio thresholds start near zero (no AI-enabled bioattack ever) but have fat tails once an engineered pandemic occurs, so severity decay per tier is shallow at long horizons; misalignment thresholds are dominated by agentic-AI deployment growth and, at the extreme tiers, loss-of-control scenarios I put at low single digits by 2100 (cross-checked against Metaculus Ragnarök figures of ~2-10% for 10% population decline via AI, and ~35%/14% community/MP for any 10% decline by 2100 — I discount those as somewhat inflated). Policy conditions are treated as exogenous risk modifiers: they barely move already-baked-in near-term, low-severity outcomes, and matter most for frontier-driven tail risk at 2030-2050; P2b/P3b (binding US+China slowdown or international licensing) cut long-horizon tail risk roughly 25-45%, P3a/P4 (US-only licensing, strict liability with scaled insurance) cut it ~15-25%, P2a (unilateral US slowdown) is weaker (~10-15%, partially offset by leakage to unconstrained jurisdictions), P1 (preemption of stricter state law) modestly raises risk (~5-10%), status quo (no further policy anywhere through 2050) raises it ~10-20% relative to unconditional (which already prices in some expected regulation), and the P5 bundle gives the largest reduction (~40-55% of tail risk at 2050, attenuated by 2100 since the measures lapse after 2050). Consistency is enforced so the all-cause AI ladder weakly dominates the union of bio/cyber/misalignment sub-ladders, and the 10%-of-population AI catastrophe sits below the corresponding deaths-only tier of the ladder.

results.title: AI Agent Security Incidents Hit 65% of Firms in 2026
results.content:
The Cloud Security Alliance and Token Security published research on April 21, 2026, titled Autonomous but Not Controlled: AI Agent Incidents Now Common in Enterprises. The headline finding is blunt: 65% of organizations have experienced at least one cybersecurity incident in the past year caused by AI agents operating on corporate networks.

## Key Takeaways [...] 2. Data exposure is the dominant failure mode. Among AI-agent-related incidents, 61% involved sensitive data exposure, 43% caused operational disruption, and 41% resulted in unintended actions across business processes. The agent isn’t “malfunctioning” — it’s doing exactly what its permissions allow. [...] Now the agent gets compromised — either through prompt injection, a supply chain attack on its upstream provider, or a credential leak. The attacker inherits everything the agent had. The Vercel breach disclosed on April 21, 2026 demonstrated exactly this pattern: attackers pivoted from a compromised third-party AI tool (Context.ai) into Vercel’s internal systems through the access the employee had granted.

# AI Agents Won’t Crash the Economy. Bad Governance Might.

As a recent report suggests, agentic AI does indeed pose risks to the white-collar economy. But we can prevent disaster, especially by acting now.

Written by Richard Ewing

Published on Mar. 09, 2026

A robotic hand manipulates a data graph showing declining profits [...] Image: Shutterstock / Built In

Brand Studio Logo

REVIEWED BY

Seth Wilson | Mar 09, 2026 [...] The market is debating whether AI agents will destroy the white-collar economy. The fear is straightforward: autonomous agents replace high-income knowledge workers, displaced workers stop spending, consumer demand contracts and, because agents do not earn wages or buy groceries, the spiral has no natural brake. In this scenario, the economy would enter a deflationary loop that compounds faster than policymakers can respond.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: AI-enabled fraud/cyber losses are already ~$1-2B+/yr reported (FBI IC3 ~$0.9B AI-assisted in 2025, deepfake fraud $1.65B in 2025, Deloitte projects $40B GenAI fraud by 2027), so cumulative low-dollar thresholds ($1B, then $10B) for AI-related and AI-cyber incidents are near-locked-in over short horizons, while death-based and $100B+ thresholds require qualitatively larger events (grid/worm-scale attacks, engineered pandemics, autonomous-agent failures) that have never occurred; the first AI-orchestrated espionage campaign (Anthropic, Nov 2025) shows capability trending up but realized damage remains modest. Bio thresholds start near zero (no AI-enabled bioattack ever) but have fat tails once an engineered pandemic occurs, so severity decay per tier is shallow at long horizons; misalignment thresholds are dominated by agentic-AI deployment growth and, at the extreme tiers, loss-of-control scenarios I put at low single digits by 2100 (cross-checked against Metaculus Ragnarök figures of ~2-10% for 10% population decline via AI, and ~35%/14% community/MP for any 10% decline by 2100 — I discount those as somewhat inflated). Policy conditions are treated as exogenous risk modifiers: they barely move already-baked-in near-term, low-severity outcomes, and matter most for frontier-driven tail risk at 2030-2050; P2b/P3b (binding US+China slowdown or international licensing) cut long-horizon tail risk roughly 25-45%, P3a/P4 (US-only licensing, strict liability with scaled insurance) cut it ~15-25%, P2a (unilateral US slowdown) is weaker (~10-15%, partially offset by leakage to unconstrained jurisdictions), P1 (preemption of stricter state law) modestly raises risk (~5-10%), status quo (no further policy anywhere through 2050) raises it ~10-20% relative to unconditional (which already prices in some expected regulation), and the P5 bundle gives the largest reduction (~40-55% of tail risk at 2050, attenuated by 2100 since the measures lapse after 2050). Consistency is enforced so the all-cause AI ladder weakly dominates the union of bio/cyber/misalignment sub-ladders, and the 10%-of-population AI catastrophe sits below the corresponding deaths-only tier of the ladder.

Bio thresholds start near zero (no AI-enabled bioattack ever) but have fat tails once an engineered pandemic occurs, so severity decay per tier is shallow at long horizons; misalignment thresholds are dominated by agentic-AI deployment growth and, at the extreme tiers, loss-of-control scenarios I put at low single digits by 2100 (cross-checked against Metaculus Ragnarök figures of ~2-10% for 10% population decline via AI, and ~35%/14% community/MP for any 10% decline by 2100 — I discount those as somewhat inflated). Consistency is enforced so the all-cause AI ladder weakly dominates the union of bio/cyber/misalignment sub-ladders, and the 10%-of-population AI catastrophe sits below the corresponding deaths-only tier of the ladder.

Policy conditions are treated as exogenous risk modifiers: they barely move already-baked-in near-term, low-severity outcomes, and matter most for frontier-driven tail risk at 2030-2050; P2b/P3b (binding US+China slowdown or international licensing) cut long-horizon tail risk roughly 25-45%, P3a/P4 (US-only licensing, strict liability with scaled insurance) cut it ~15-25%, P2a (unilateral US slowdown) is weaker (~10-15%, partially offset by leakage to unconstrained jurisdictions), P1 (preemption of stricter state law) modestly raises risk (~5-10%), status quo (no further policy anywhere through 2050) raises it ~10-20% relative to unconditional (which already prices in some expected regulation), and the P5 bundle gives the largest reduction (~40-55% of tail risk at 2050, attenuated by 2100 since the measures lapse after 2050). Consistency is enforced so the all-cause AI ladder weakly dominates the union of bio/cyber/misalignment sub-ladders, and the 10%-of-population AI catastrophe sits below the corresponding deaths-only tier of the ladder.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Anchors: (1) The AI-cyber ladder is already near-certain at low severity — Anthropic's Nov 2025 GTG-1002 AI-orchestrated campaign plus IBM 2026 data ($6M avg AI-enabled breach × thousands of breaches, 56% YoY rise in AI-driven attacks) means cumulative AI-related cyber damages ≥$1B are effectively realized; hence cyber:100 and ai:100 are ~0.85–0.99 even short-term. (2) FRI LEAP Wave 9 (May–Jun 2026): median expert 62% / superforecaster 70% for an AI event ≥50 deaths OR $100B by 2050, with conditional timing 25% by 2031 and 50% by 2035 — this pins the ai:1k–ai:10k band. (3) LEAP AI-catastrophe (≥10% population): slow 0.08%/1%/2% and rapid 1%/5%/10% by 2030/2050/2100; I blend to ~0.6%/3.5%/7.5% for catastrophe:ai, with catastrophe:general modestly higher (adds pandemic/nuclear). The "ai" category is the union and dominates the sub-ladders; cyber leads at low severity while misalignment and bio dominate the extreme tail growth by 2050–2100. Severity ladders decline steeply (roughly 3–5x per 10x threshold) and rise with horizon. Bio requires deliberate human/AI pathogen processing (rarer, lower base rate). Disempowerment tracks loss-of-control trajectories. Policy effects are modest and roughly hold across the ladder: SQ slightly above unconditional; P1 (ceiling preemption) marginally raises risk; slowdown/pre-release/strict-liability (P2b/P3/P4) each cut tail risk ~15–35%; the P5 bundle cuts most (~50–70% at high severity, concentrated in misalignment/large-scale where governance bites, less at low-severity cyber which is driven by diffuse misuse unaffected by frontier controls).

results.title: 2026 IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report: The $6M AI threat no ...
results.content:
A data breach now costs $1,100 for every hour it stays unresolved. In 2026, breaches averaged 247 days to contain, adding up to a record $4.99 million per incident. According to IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report, produced with Ponemon Institute from 602 breached organizations across 16 countries, this year's data reveals one critical theme: AI threats have become the deciding factor in breach economics. [...] ### Shadow AI

Shadow AI, meaning AI tools employees adopt without security approval, accounted for 43% of AI-related incidents in 2026, more than double the 20% recorded the prior year. Roughly one in five of these incidents resulted in a regulatory fine, and only about a third of organizations enforce strict approval processes for deploying AI tools internally.

### Non-human identities [...] IBM's 2026 report describes asymmetric acceleration. Attackers are adopting AI faster in the areas that hurt most, while defenders deploy their best tools everywhere except the front door. The 18% vulnerability gap, the 92% access control failure rate, and the 85% reckoning all point to the same conclusion: the breach economics equation has shifted, and speed is now the variable that decides the outcome.

More than 471 million million victim notices were associated with data compromises in the first half of 2026, according to a new report from the Identity Theft Resource Center, a nonprofit that assists identity-theft victims and tracks publicly reported data breaches. A cyber incident that occurred at education tool Canvas accounted for more than half of those notices, at 275 million. [...] The half-year tally compares with 297.5 million notices issued in all of 2025, the ITRC report shows. The number of incidents reached 1,803 in the first half of the year, up from 1,732 during the same period in 2025. If the second half of the year is as active, the final tally for 2026 will eclipse the 3,321 security incidents reported for all of last year.

## Read more CNBC personal finance coverage [...] Key Points

result.answer: In 2026, AI experts estimate a 20% probability of an AI-driven existential catastrophe, with views ranging widely from near 0% to over 90%. The estimates have increased since 2020. There is no consensus among experts.

results.title: P(doom) Survey 2026: What Do AI Researchers Think?
results.content:
// Key Findings

 Median estimate: ~20% probability of existential catastrophe from AI across all sources
 Estimates range from near 0% (LeCun, Ng) to >90% (some EA-aligned researchers)
 AI safety researchers estimate significantly higher P(doom) than mainstream ML researchers
 Estimates have increased on average since 2020 across all groups
 No consensus: the standard deviation across estimates is larger than the median itself

// Distribution Summary

Median Estimate

Mean Estimate

~25% [...] P(doom) is the estimated probability that advanced AI leads to human extinction or permanent civilisational collapse. The term was popularised in AI safety circles — particularly by researchers at MIRI and associated organisations — and is now widely used by researchers, forecasters, and journalists to communicate a single-number summary of long-term AI existential risk. [...] Limitations: P(doom) is not a standardised metric. Different researchers define the term differently — some include economic collapse or loss of human autonomy, others only biological extinction. Estimates are point-in-time and may have changed. This is a descriptive survey, not an endorsement of any estimate or a claim about the actual probability of AI catastrophe.

Updates: This report will be updated annually. Last updated June 2026.

results.title: Why do Experts Disagree on Existential Risk and P(doom) ...
results.content: Several existing surveys have examined AI expert beliefs. The largest is the AI Impacts Survey(Grace et al., 2024), which surveys thousands of authors at the NeurIPS conference. AI Impacts asked experts questions such as “when will AI exceed human performance,” in response, the median expert answered 2061, and 10% answered 2026. According to AI Impacts, roughly 40% of respondents indicated a >10% chance of catastrophic outcomes from AI progress. Other surveys also seek to answer when experts [...] Prominent AI researchers hold dramatically different views on the degree of risk from building AGI. For example, Dr. Roman Yampolskiy estimates a 99% chance of an AI-caused existential catastrophe[Dr. Roman Yampolskiy [@romanyam] (2024)](#bib.bib4) (often called “P(doom)”) whereas others such as Yann Lecun believe that this probability is effectively zero[Yann LeCun [@ylecun] (2023)](#bib.bib5). The goal of the survey is to understand what drives this massive divergence in views on AI risk [...] My survey collected responses from 111 AI professionals across academia, industry, and AI safety research. As shown in Figure 1? A Survey of AI Experts"), most of the respondents (66.3%) were academic researchers, followed by industry professionals (16.3%) and AI safety researchers (9.3%), while the rest (8.1%) fell into other category.

results.title: Views on AI Existential Risk Before and After a Public ...
results.content:

This post covers key highlights from the Wave 9 LEAP survey that we conducted between May 19 and June 10, 2026. Recent waves covered robotics, the economic effects of AI, security and geopolitics, AI R&D, and AI timelines. More information about Wave 9, including question details and analysis of rationales, is available here.

### Insight 1: Experts and superforecasters think a major AI-driven harm event is more likely than not by 2050 [...] We also asked respondents for the probability of a global catastrophe from any cause—again defining catastrophe as the death of more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period. Conditional on AI capabilities progressing rapidly by 2030, the median expert forecasts the probability of an AI-related catastrophe by 2100 at 10% compared with 15% for a catastrophe from any cause. [...] We also asked forecasters to predict the likelihood of a global AI-related catastrophe in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period. If AI capabilities progress slowly, the median expert assigns this a 0.08% probability by 2030, 1% by 2050, and 2% by 2100. In a scenario where AI progress by 2030 is rapid, those forecasts rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%.1

UPDATED 17:51 EDT / NOVEMBER 13 2025

### Anthropic reveals first reported ‘AI-orchestrated cyber espionage’ campaign using Claude

by  Duncan Riley

Artificial intelligence company Anthropic PBC today provided details of what it says is the first reported “AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign.” [...] The campaign involved alleged Chinese state-sponsored hackers using Anthropic’s Claude model to automate major portions of a cyber espionage campaign targeting dozens of global organizations. The company says the attackers orchestrated reconnaissance, exploit development and data exfiltration with minimal human involvement, marking one of the clearest examples yet of an AI agent operating as the core engine of an intrusion. [...] The attackers bypassed safeguards in the Claude AI model by framing their prompts as penetration-testing tasks and breaking malicious instructions into smaller subtasks that appeared benign. Anthropic says the actor effectively “social-engineered” the system’s guardrails, enabling automated progression through each phase of the intrusion.

The company did not identify the victims but said the activity aligns with a “well-resourced, state-sponsored group” operating out of China.

condition.label: Federal preemption of state AI laws

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Anchors: (1) The AI-cyber ladder is already near-certain at low severity — Anthropic's Nov 2025 GTG-1002 AI-orchestrated campaign plus IBM 2026 data ($6M avg AI-enabled breach × thousands of breaches, 56% YoY rise in AI-driven attacks) means cumulative AI-related cyber damages ≥$1B are effectively realized; hence cyber:100 and ai:100 are ~0.85–0.99 even short-term. (2) FRI LEAP Wave 9 (May–Jun 2026): median expert 62% / superforecaster 70% for an AI event ≥50 deaths OR $100B by 2050, with conditional timing 25% by 2031 and 50% by 2035 — this pins the ai:1k–ai:10k band. (3) LEAP AI-catastrophe (≥10% population): slow 0.08%/1%/2% and rapid 1%/5%/10% by 2030/2050/2100; I blend to ~0.6%/3.5%/7.5% for catastrophe:ai, with catastrophe:general modestly higher (adds pandemic/nuclear). The "ai" category is the union and dominates the sub-ladders; cyber leads at low severity while misalignment and bio dominate the extreme tail growth by 2050–2100. Severity ladders decline steeply (roughly 3–5x per 10x threshold) and rise with horizon. Bio requires deliberate human/AI pathogen processing (rarer, lower base rate). Disempowerment tracks loss-of-control trajectories. Policy effects are modest and roughly hold across the ladder: SQ slightly above unconditional; P1 (ceiling preemption) marginally raises risk; slowdown/pre-release/strict-liability (P2b/P3/P4) each cut tail risk ~15–35%; the P5 bundle cuts most (~50–70% at high severity, concentrated in misalignment/large-scale where governance bites, less at low-severity cyber which is driven by diffuse misuse unaffected by frontier controls).

condition.label: Pre-release authorization: international body incl. US + China

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Anchors: (1) The AI-cyber ladder is already near-certain at low severity — Anthropic's Nov 2025 GTG-1002 AI-orchestrated campaign plus IBM 2026 data ($6M avg AI-enabled breach × thousands of breaches, 56% YoY rise in AI-driven attacks) means cumulative AI-related cyber damages ≥$1B are effectively realized; hence cyber:100 and ai:100 are ~0.85–0.99 even short-term. (2) FRI LEAP Wave 9 (May–Jun 2026): median expert 62% / superforecaster 70% for an AI event ≥50 deaths OR $100B by 2050, with conditional timing 25% by 2031 and 50% by 2035 — this pins the ai:1k–ai:10k band. (3) LEAP AI-catastrophe (≥10% population): slow 0.08%/1%/2% and rapid 1%/5%/10% by 2030/2050/2100; I blend to ~0.6%/3.5%/7.5% for catastrophe:ai, with catastrophe:general modestly higher (adds pandemic/nuclear). The "ai" category is the union and dominates the sub-ladders; cyber leads at low severity while misalignment and bio dominate the extreme tail growth by 2050–2100. Severity ladders decline steeply (roughly 3–5x per 10x threshold) and rise with horizon. Bio requires deliberate human/AI pathogen processing (rarer, lower base rate). Disempowerment tracks loss-of-control trajectories. Policy effects are modest and roughly hold across the ladder: SQ slightly above unconditional; P1 (ceiling preemption) marginally raises risk; slowdown/pre-release/strict-liability (P2b/P3/P4) each cut tail risk ~15–35%; the P5 bundle cuts most (~50–70% at high severity, concentrated in misalignment/large-scale where governance bites, less at low-severity cyber which is driven by diffuse misuse unaffected by frontier controls).

results.content:
A new paper published in June 2026, Prioritizing the Risks from Artificial Intelligence, reports findings from a three-round Delphi study conducted with 272 international AI experts in late 2025. Rather than cataloging AI risks in abstract terms, the study asked experts to assign concrete probability estimates to 24 risk domains, identify which sectors and actors are most vulnerable, and name who bears primary responsibility for doing something about it. [...] The headline finding is striking. Under a business-as-usual scenario, defined as organizations and governments continuing existing practices without implementing additional AI-specific risk mitigations, experts assessed a greater than 10% probability of catastrophic outcomes from 18 of 24 AI risk domains over the next five years. [...] Under most standard risk governance frameworks, including ISO 31000 and the NIST AI RMF, a 10% probability of catastrophic harm over a five-year horizon is considered “intolerable.”. Eighteen of twenty-four AI risk domains cross that line under current conditions.

results.title: These are the most urgent AI risks, according to 272 experts

Catastrophic outcomes were defined as harms that include the potential for more than 1 million deaths, more than $100 billion in financial losses, or comparable civilizational-scale intangible damages. [...] The experts identified five risks — dangerous capabilities, competitive pressures, weapons and cyberattacks, concentrated power, and false information — as the most likely to produce the most severe harms over the next five years. The information and finance sectors are especially vulnerable, the experts said, and the people and organizations most vulnerable to risks are often not best positioned to address them. [...] The study used the Delphi method, a structured research process that gathers expert judgments over multiple rounds to move toward clearer areas of agreement and disagreement. The researchers used those expert assessments to evaluate risks over a five-year horizon, from 2025 to 2030, under two scenarios: business as usual, in which organizations and governments continue their current paths, and pragmatic mitigation, in which they make cost-effective efforts to reduce AI risks.

results.content: Catastrophes occur even when competitive pressures are low, as in the examples of the nuclear disasters of Chernobyl and the Three Mile Island, as well as the accidental release of anthrax in Sverdlovsk. For example, extreme inequality can be exacerbated by AI technologies that [...] Malicious use: People could intentionally harness powerful AIs to cause widespread harm. AI could be used to engineer new pandemics or for propaganda, censorship, and surveillance, or released to autonomously pursue harmful goals. To reduce these risks, we suggest improving biosecurity, restricting access to dangerous AI models, and holding AI developers liable for harms.

results.title: AI Threats & Board-Level Cyber Risk Decisions 2026
results.content:
### Updating Cyber Risk Reporting Frameworks for AI Threats

Most board dashboards were designed around historical indicators: incident counts, patching cadence, phishing click rates, and mean time to detect. Those remain relevant, but they no longer fully describe exposure in an AI-enabled environment. [...] Most enterprise cyber governance structures were designed for threats that scaled linearly. AI-driven cyber attacks do not scale linearly. This is where many board-level cyber risk decisions are becoming misaligned with operational reality.

### Assumptions Built for Pre-AI Threat Models

Traditional cyber risk governance frameworks assume:

 Human-driven attack cadence
 Observable dwell time before impact
 Clear separation between reconnaissance, exploitation, and monetization phases [...] Many organizations maintain incident response retainers structured around forensic investigation and advisory support. Those models often assume time for scoping and staged escalation. But AI-driven cyber attacks compress that window.

results.title: Legal and Policy Approaches to Mitigate Catastrophic ...
results.content:
Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have raised fears of catastrophic harms, such as cyberattacks and bioweapon misuse. To explore ways to reduce these risks, RAND researchers held a Delphi study with 24 U.S. AI and policy experts. Participants saw few feasible policy options, favoring risk disclosure incentives and voluntary safety standards over strict regulation. Near-term progress may rely on state and industry action. [...] The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models has generated growing concern about their potential to cause catastrophic harms, including cyberattacks, bioweapon misuse, and loss of human control. Despite numerous governmental, nongovernmental, and industry efforts to establish safeguards, the effectiveness of various legal and policy measures in mitigating such risks remains uncertain. [...] The findings suggest that comprehensive federal action to mitigate catastrophic AI risks is unlikely in the near term. Instead, progress may depend on state-level initiatives and voluntary measures by industry and nongovernmental actors. Although even the most promising approaches have limitations, targeted mechanisms, such as structured disclosure programs and legal safe harbors for researchers, could enhance their effectiveness in promoting AI safety and accountability.

Policies reduce risk via capability slowdown (p2), vetting (p3), and safety incentives from liability/insurance (p4); p5 bundle cuts probs most (~50-70% relative reduction), p1 slightly elevates by limiting stricter state rules, sq exceeds unconditional as no expected policies. Short-horizon probs near-zero for high severities; all assume perfect knowledge of causation.

rationale: I started from base rates: no clearly AI-caused mass-casualty event has yet occurred, but cyber losses are now frequently AI-enabled at ordinary breach scales, while engineered-biological and loss-of-control pathways dominate the extreme tail. Near-term probabilities are therefore driven mostly by AI-enabled cyber/economic damage; by 2050 and 2100 the ladder increasingly reflects frontier-capability, biorisk, autonomous-agent, and disempowerment scenarios. I treated status quo/no-new-policy and federal preemption as somewhat risk-increasing relative to the unconditional path because I expect some additional safety policy otherwise; bilateral slowdown, international pre-release authorization, and the bundled policy reduce risk most, especially for frontier-AI and misalignment-driven tails. For all-cause global catastrophe, I used XPT-like all-risk base rates and adjusted only the AI component under AI-policy conditions, so policy effects are smaller than on AI-specific questions.

Near-term probabilities are therefore driven mostly by AI-enabled cyber/economic damage; by 2050 and 2100 the ladder increasingly reflects frontier-capability, biorisk, autonomous-agent, and disempowerment scenarios. I treated status quo/no-new-policy and federal preemption as somewhat risk-increasing relative to the unconditional path because I expect some additional safety policy otherwise; bilateral slowdown, international pre-release authorization, and the bundled policy reduce risk most, especially for frontier-AI and misalignment-driven tails. For all-cause global catastrophe, I used XPT-like all-risk base rates and adjusted only the AI component under AI-policy conditions, so policy effects are smaller than on AI-specific questions.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: AI-enabled cyber/fraud losses are already ~$1-3B/yr globally (FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-assisted crime losses in 2025 alone; deepfake fraud ~$1.65B in 2025), so with the perfect-knowledge clause the lowest rungs ($1B cumulative) are near-certain over multi-year horizons and likely even within 6-12 months, while precedent (NotPetya ~$10B, COVID ~$10T+) anchors what larger rungs require. AI-caused epidemics and true loss-of-control incidents have essentially no track record at scale, so short-horizon probabilities are small and rise with capability growth (agentic deployment, bio-uplift) toward 2050/2100; the AI-any ladder is set at roughly the union of the bio/cyber/misalignment ladders plus other channels (autonomous systems, AI-triggered escalation). Cross-checks: Metaculus community puts ~35% on a 10% population decline in 5 years by 2100; I discount that heavily to ~13% for a single causally-linked catastrophe, with an AI-proximate 10%-mortality catastrophe at ~6% by 2100 and disempowerment at ~22% (dominated by gradual/hard-to-avert scenarios late-century). Policy conditions shift risk modestly: near-term effects are minimal because current models already suffice for the low rungs, while by 2030-2050 stringent regimes (P2b joint slowdown, P3b international licensing, P4 strict liability, and especially the P5 bundle) cut mid/high-severity and misalignment risk by ~20-50%, with partial attenuation by 2100 after the 2050 sunset; the status quo (no new policy) and federal preemption (P1) raise long-horizon risk slightly relative to unconditional, and a US-only slowdown (P2a) helps less because it does not bind China.

results.title: Data breaches surge in 2026 as AI plays a growing role ...
results.content:
More than 471 million million victim notices were associated with data compromises in the first half of 2026, according to a new report from the Identity Theft Resource Center, a nonprofit that assists identity-theft victims and tracks publicly reported data breaches. A cyber incident that occurred at education tool Canvas accounted for more than half of those notices, at 275 million. [...] Additionally, the ITRC report notes that some organizations have been targeted by a scam the FBI has flagged in which North Korea places remote information technology workers in U.S. businesses using stolen identities, deepfake videos during interviews and AI-generated resumes. "This is arguably the most significant structural driver of malicious insider attacks," the report reads. [...] The half-year tally compares with 297.5 million notices issued in all of 2025, the ITRC report shows. The number of incidents reached 1,803 in the first half of the year, up from 1,732 during the same period in 2025. If the second half of the year is as active, the final tally for 2026 will eclipse the 3,321 security incidents reported for all of last year.

results.title: The biggest cyber breaches of 2026 so far
results.content:
Threat intelligence reports show attackers moving faster than ever. Some cybercriminal groups can break into networks and begin spreading laterally in under 30 seconds. AI-assisted attacks are rising sharply, and zero-day vulnerabilities are being exploited faster than security teams can respond.

But here’s the uncomfortable truth:

Many of the biggest cybersecurity breaches in 2026 so far weren’t unstoppable attacks. They were preventable failures. [...] Read: Common cybersecurity myths debunked

Below are some of the largest cybersecurity incidents of 2026 so far, along with the key lessons they reveal about cybersecurity training.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

## What the Attack Reveals About the Agentic AI Attack Surface [...] The OWASP Agentic Top 10, released in December 2025, ranks identity and privilege abuse (ASI03) and agent goal hijacking (ASI01) among its top risks precisely because agents amplify the consequences of every over-permissioned credential and every missing access boundary. results.title: If there is an artificial intelligence catastrophe this century, when will it happen?
If, before 2050, AI kills more than 1 million people, will the policy response be insufficient?
Before 2032, will we see an event precipitated by AI malfunction that causes at least 100 deaths and/or at least $1B 2021 USD in economic damage?

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

condition.label: Federal preemption of state AI laws

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

rationale: Low-severity thresholds ($1B / 100 deaths) for AI-broad and AI-cyber are near-certain even short-term: FBI IC3 logged ~$893M in AI-enabled losses in 2025 alone, IBM finds ~1-in-4 breaches AI-enabled, and Anthropic documented a largely-autonomous AI cyber-espionage campaign (Sept-Nov 2025), so cumulative $1B AI-attributable damage is effectively already crossed. Probabilities fall steeply with severity (roughly power-law), with cyber and broad-AI categories dominating mid-tier thresholds and bio dominating some upper-tail mass owing to documented novice-uplift concerns; mass-casualty (100k+) events remain rare and back-loaded to 2050/2100. For catastrophe/x-risk I anchor between superforecaster medians (very low: ~0.0001% 2030 extinction) and AI-expert/domain medians (~3% 2100 extinction), setting the 10%-population AI catastrophe near 0.6%/5%/12% and disempowerment somewhat higher since it needn't involve mass death. Policy effects: I treat implementation as exogenous (not signal of a riskier world), so SQ is modestly above unconditional at long horizons and stringent bundles (P5, then P2b/P3b, then P4) cut tail risk materially—most for misalignment and disempowerment where governance directly bites—while P1 (preemption, a regulatory ceiling) slightly raises risk; effects are negligible at 6-12mo and for already-saturated low thresholds. Misalignment tail and disempowerment show the largest policy sensitivity because binding US-China slowdown plus international pre-release authorization plausibly removes a large share of loss-of-control probability mass.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Anchors: (1) Low ladder rungs for AI/cyber are near-certain on economic thresholds — IBM/FBI data show AI-enabled cyber losses already ~$1B/yr and growing 89%/yr, so $1B cumulative resolves quickly; $10B within a few years is likely. (2) FRI's AI-cyber pilot implies very thin tails for $1T+ cyber damages near-term but substantial cumulative probability by 2050. (3) Bio ladder uses FRI LLM-biorisk anchors (~0.3–1.5%/yr AI-uplifted human-caused epidemic risk) with fat conditional severity tails (engineered pandemics scale like COVID or worse). (4) Misalignment ladder reflects rapidly expanding agentic deployment; $1B-scale specification-gaming/agent failures become likely by 2030, with tail probabilities anchored to XPT/Metaculus AI-catastrophe estimates (catastrophe:ai 2100 ≈ 5.5%, between XPT superforecasters and experts given observed AI progress outpacing XPT expectations). Catastrophe:general (~11% by 2100) sits near XPT superforecaster/Metaculus medians. Policy conditions: effects scale with horizon and severity; P1 (preemption) mildly increases risk (~+5% relative at tails); SQ raises long-horizon risk ~15-20% relative vs unconditional (which anticipates some future regulation); P2a/P3a/P4 each cut tail risk ~10-25%; P2b/P3b ~25-35% (China inclusion matters most); P5 bundle cuts 2050 tails roughly in half and disempowerment by ~60% at 2050, with attenuation by 2100 since policies lapse in 2050. Near-term (6-12mo) effects are small because current-generation capabilities and deployed systems already drive most short-run risk.

results.content:
Ninety-two percent lacking proper AI access controls is not a rounding error. It’s a structural failure that shows up across every AI-related incident type the report tracked. Model inversion attacks, where an attacker extracts sensitive data by probing a model’s outputs, averaged USD 6.07 million per breach — 18% above the global average. Prompt injection incidents came in close behind at USD 5.89 million. Cloud misconfigurations affecting AI workloads cost USD 5.25 million. None of these are [...] IBM and the Ponemon Institute released the 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report this month, the 21st edition of a study that has tracked breach economics since 2005. The global average cost of a breach climbed to USD 4.99 million, a 12% jump over last year and a new record. That number will lead most of the coverage. It shouldn’t. The number that matters is buried on page 40: 92% of organizations that experienced an AI-related security incident lacked proper AI access controls when it happened. [...] 1. Global breach costs hit a record USD 4.99 million. That’s a 12% increase over last year, reversing a rare dip in 2025 and continuing an upward trend that has held since the pandemic.
2. AI adoption without governance, not AI itself, is the primary cost driver. Among organizations that suffered an AI-related breach, 92% lacked proper AI access controls, and those incidents averaged USD 5.33 million versus USD 4.70 million for breaches that didn’t involve AI.

results.title: Data breaches surge in 2026 as AI plays a growing role ...
results.content:
More than 471 million million victim notices were associated with data compromises in the first half of 2026, according to a new report from the Identity Theft Resource Center, a nonprofit that assists identity-theft victims and tracks publicly reported data breaches. A cyber incident that occurred at education tool Canvas accounted for more than half of those notices, at 275 million. [...] "We continue to see this ever-increasing number of data breaches," said James Lee, president of the ITRC. "That does not appear to be slowing down."

## AI involved in more breaches

The increase in data breaches comes as artificial intelligence's ever-improving capabilities make it easier to exploit vulnerabilities in company systems. Between March 2025 and February 2026, one in four breaches was AI-enabled, up 56% from a year earlier, according to a new study from IBM. [...] Additionally, the ITRC report notes that some organizations have been targeted by a scam the FBI has flagged in which North Korea places remote information technology workers in U.S. businesses using stolen identities, deepfake videos during interviews and AI-generated resumes. "This is arguably the most significant structural driver of malicious insider attacks," the report reads.

results.content:
The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) aimed to produce high-quality forecasts of the risks facing humanity over the next century by incentivizing thoughtful forecasts, explanations, persuasion, and updating from 169 forecasters over a multi-stage tournament. In this first iteration of the XPT, we discover points where historically accurate forecasters on short-run questions (superforecasters) and domain experts agree and disagree in their probability estimates of short-, medium-, and [...] What are the gravest risks facing humanity over the next century and beyond? In 2022, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) brought together 80 experts and 89 superforecasters to predict the risks to humanity posed by artificial intelligence, nuclear war, pandemics, and other causes.

We document large-scale disagreement and minimal convergence of beliefs over the course of the XPT, with the largest disagreement about risks from artificial intelligence. rationale: Base rates from expert surveys (e.g. ~1% median for AI global cat by 2030 rising to 5-10% by 2050 in rapid scenarios; MIT ~20% for dangerous capabilities/mass harm by ~2030; cyber top risk per Allianz 2026) inform low near-term severe probs that ladder down with severity and up with time. Lower thresholds (e.g. $1B cyber) have higher probs due to "or" economic clause and current trends in AI-intensified incidents. Unconditional assumes moderate policy tightening (some federal oversight). SQ raises probs ~20-40% (less mitigation). P1 mildly raises (blocks stricter states). P2a/b, P3a/b, P4 reduce 30-70% via slowing/vetting/liability incentives (strongest for p5 bundle ~60-80% cut). Bio/misalign rarer than cyber near-term. Global cat/disempowerment aligned to expert medians ~1-5% by 2030, 5-15% 2050 for AI. All respect perfect knowledge, excess mortality, but-for AI role.
